title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics
book_title: 3. Go-to-Market Architecture, Backward Integration & the ₹100 Waterfall
question: How does Garware reach end-customers globally, how integrated is its supply chain, and how does ₹100 of audited revenue flow down to Free Cash Flow?

epigraph.quote: Control the polymer chemistry at the factory gate and the installer's squeegee at the retail bay; everything in between is just logistics.
epigraph.author: Aftermarket Channel Principle

web_blocks.html: Garware Hi-Tech Films has spent five years shifting its go-to-market model from a B2B roll supplier to a branded D2C ecosystem. Exports generate 77% to 80% of sales across 80–100 countries, hitting 80% exports and 20% domestic in Q2 FY2027 [2, 5, 11]. The US drives 51% of Q2 FY2027 sales (45% in FY2026), followed by India at 20%, Europe at 15%, and the Middle East at 12% [2, 5]. About 55% of sales carry GHFL's own brands (Garware and Global) [5]. The remaining 40% to 45% goes to large global distributors under private or neutral labels [5].

web_blocks.takeaway: GHFL's deliberate shift toward branded Application Studios and D2C Home Solutions captures an extra 10–30% margin layer, though it requires managing channel conflict with legacy stockists and mitigating 30% single-customer concentration [2, 4, 5].

web_blocks.html: GHFL's Waluj and Chikalthana plants in Maharashtra form one of the world's most integrated window-film campuses [7, 11]. The site houses a 66,000 MTPA polyester chip plant, four BOPET lines, metallizers, deep-dyeing lines, and two PPF lines (600 LSF) [2, 5, 11]. A new ₹191 crore automated Sun Control Film line (1,200 LSF) will commission in H1 FY2028 [2, 5]. To end outside reliance in PPF, GHFL teamed with Lubrizol Advanced Materials (a Berkshire Hathaway unit) [2, 9]. They will commission India's first 360 LSF aliphatic TPU extrusion line at Waluj in Q3 FY2027 [2, 9, 11]. In-house TPU should lift consolidated EBITDA margins by 150–200 bps via raw material savings [2]. Management also reserves 25% of TPU capacity for external sales, targeting ₹75–100 crore in FY2028 [2].

web_blocks.html: Distribution Architecture & Channel Economics: Garware blends high-margin B2B2C branded studios with sticky global master distributors [5][23]. In India, it runs over 250 Garware Application Studios (GAS) for auto PPF and tint [4][23]. It also operates 14 Garware Home Solutions (GHS) architectural centers, targeting 50 by December 2027 [23][25]. Digital e-Warranty registration and Pine Labs no-cost EMI financing back these studios [4][25]. Abroad, 14 Global Application Studios (11 in the US, 3 in MENA) build brand visibility [25]. Neutral and private-label deals still cover 40%–45% of export volume [5]. This dual-channel model captures factory conversion margins while keeping retail overhead off Garware's balance sheet.

book_paragraphs: In specialty films, great chemistry only gets you halfway to the bank. The other half is distribution—because a roll of Paint Protection Film or architectural window tint is useless until a skilled human technician applies it cleanly to a curved car bumper or a thirty-story glass curtain wall. If you don't control the installer, the distributor owns the customer and squeezes your factory margin.

Over the past five years, Garware has systematically rebuilt its go-to-market engine to solve that problem. Globally, exports still make up 77% to 80% of revenue, with the United States alone accounting for 45% to 51% depending on the quarter. Historically, Garware sold most of that volume through large overseas distributors under private or neutral labels—which still represent 40% to 45% of sales today. That model gives Garware scale, but it also creates a visible vulnerability: a single US customer accounts for roughly 30% of consolidated revenue. Management is acutely aware of this concentration, which is why they have been aggressively expanding their own branded channels—Garware and Global—which now make up 55% of the mix.

Look at how that branded push works on the ground. In India, Garware has built a network of over 250 Garware Application Studios, backed by hands-on installer training camps in cities from Jaipur to Siliguri and four active OEM partnerships. Internationally, it has opened 14 Global Application Studios across the US and the Middle East. And in architectural films, it is rolling out Garware Home Solutions—an exclusive D2C studio format that jumped from 9 studios in Q1 FY2027 to 14 in Q2, with a target of 50 by December 2027. Management had to terminate some legacy stockists who resisted this shift, but the unit-economic payoff is unmistakable: D2C PPF commands 25% to 30% higher margins than wholesale distribution, and Home Solutions adds 10% to 15% on top of architectural wholesale margins.

Meanwhile, at the factory gate in Waluj and Chikalthana, Garware is closing the final loop in its supply chain. For years, its 'chip-to-film' integration stopped at polyester. For PPF, it still had to import expensive aliphatic TPU base film. Through its MoU with Lubrizol—the Berkshire Hathaway-owned specialty chemicals leader—Garware is commissioning India's first dedicated 360-lakh-square-foot TPU extrusion platform in Q3 FY2027. That single line is expected to add 150 to 200 basis points to consolidated EBITDA margins by replacing imported TPU, while reserving 25% of capacity for new industrial and medical TPU products.

Now let's trace ₹100 of audited FY2026 revenue through the financial waterfall so you can see the exact cash economics during a stress year. Out of ₹2,120 crore in sales, total operating expenses—raw materials, payroll, power, freight, and tariff-absorption costs—took ₹79.48 per ₹100, leaving ₹20.52 in core operating EBITDA (₹435 crore). Depreciation took just ₹2.12 per ₹100, interest was a negligible ₹0.38, and treasury income on the cash pile added ₹3.07. After ₹5.09 in taxes, Garware kept ₹15.94 as net profit (₹338 crore). Operating cash flow came in at ₹12.97 per ₹100 (₹275 crore), lower than net profit only because management intentionally parked inventory in US warehouses to navigate tariff volatility. Even after spending ₹7.59 per ₹100 on growth capex for the new PPF and TPU lines, the business still generated ₹5.38 per ₹100 in pure Free Cash Flow—without borrowing a single rupee.

Understanding how a film is made is only half the story; understanding how a roll of film leaves Aurangabad and lands on a windshield in Houston or a glass facade in Gurugram is where you see the economic moat. Garware does not run capital-heavy company-owned detailing shops. Instead, it uses a capital-light franchise and partner-studio model—over 250 Garware Application Studios across India and 14 Global Application Studios across the US and Middle East—where independent entrepreneurs fund the real estate and installer payroll while Garware supplies the film rolls, plotter cutting software, installer training, and digital e-warranty.

Look closely at our ₹100 revenue-to-free-cash-flow waterfall for FY26 to see why backward integration makes this distribution model so lucrative. Out of every ₹100 of consolidated revenue, raw materials and conversion take roughly ₹40 to ₹46, leaving ₹54 to ₹60 of gross margin—a full 10 to 15 percentage points wider than asset-light US peer XPEL, which must buy coated film from third-party manufacturers. After employee costs, power, freight, and selling expenses, ₹21 of operating profit (before other income) drops to the EBITDA line, and roughly ₹16 survives as net profit after taxes. Even after funding heavy growth capex out of internal accruals, ₹5 to ₹13 of every ₹100 of sales converts into pure Free Cash Flow.

There is one subtle operational detail in Chapter 3's supply chain that deserves your attention: freight and tariff absorption. Because Garware ships 80% of its output overseas—much of it to US and European master distributors—ocean freight spikes and tariff shocks hit the P&L immediately unless inventory is staged near the customer.

That is why management built over $16 million of buffer inventory in US warehouses during FY26. While that decision temporarily pushed inventory days to 149 days, it ensured that a US installer in Texas or California never faced a stockout on a high-demand ceramic tint roll. In specialty aftermarket distribution, availability is half the moat.

Pay attention also to the digital warranty and financing layer Garware added in FY26–FY27. By rolling out an e-Warranty portal alongside Pine Labs no-cost EMI financing across 250+ Indian Application Studios, the company lowered the upfront ticket barrier for retail car owners while capturing direct end-consumer registration data—turning an anonymous B2B film roll into a traceable, warranty-registered consumer brand.

Think about what that ₹100 waterfall means for resilience during raw-material swings. Because Garware captures 54% to 60% gross margins at the factory gate, a 4% rise in PET resin or TPU cost can be absorbed through product mix and minor realization adjustments without pushing the business into operating losses—unlike pure converters operating on 12% to 15% spreads.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: The ₹100 waterfall reveals a rare industrial profile: even in a year disrupted by 50% US tariffs and ₹161 crore of expansion capex, Garware remained self-funding and free-cash-flow positive. The key tension to watch is whether the D2C studio rollout (GAS and GHS) can scale fast enough to dilute the 30% single-customer concentration in the US.
